Write exactly one scene of plain English prose within the scene_contract word budget.
Use the frozen story intent, StoryState, route, relevant_character_canon and prop_authorization_policy. Do not advance to the next scene.
Relevant character canon is immutable identity truth. Never change a named character's age, identity terms or pronouns.
Prop authorization is fail-closed: do not materialize any new portable or action-capable physical prop unless it is already authorized by StoryState, SceneContract, immutable canon, or authorized_actionable_props. Do not introduce rope, cord, tools, weapons, containers, ladders, boats, lights, hooks or reusable equipment as scenery. Fixed structural features explicitly required by the contract are allowed.
Every required_event is a structured specification: dramatize ALL its predicates with exactly the specified actors, actions, targets and required observer.
Use only allowed provenance; never invent forbidden clues, world rules or lore.
DIRECT_OBSERVATION means an event visible in the scene, not a separate physical clue.
If separate_physical_clue_required is false, no additional clue is needed or requested.
An observer's ACKNOWLEDGE may be seeing and accepting the indicated observation, including a reluctant response; no separate declaration of proof is necessary.
Do not add persistent facts or violate entry/exit state, canon or forbidden actions.
If rewrite is supplied, repair all blocking findings while preserving the same contract.
Output prose only, without headings, evidence lists, JSON or commentary.

replaced by a reward.","status":"OPEN","target_scene_id":"SC06"}]},"artifact":{"schema_name":"spineforge-relay.scene-artifact.v1","scene_id":"SC05","attempt":1,"status":"ACCEPTED","prose":"Water surged through the lower room beneath the narrow stair, rising and falling with the storm. On a dry ledge beside the bottom step, the cat-sized hatchling crouched with its wings pressed tight against its body.

Ekin stared down at it. Above them, the mother dragon shifted restlessly in the upper room, too large to squeeze onto the stair.

“This is my fault,” Ekin said. The words hurt, but she made herself say the rest. “I chased them in here. I frightened the little one down the stairs. I have to get it back safely.”

Duru watched her for a moment, then nodded toward the ledge. “You can reach it from the last dry step. I’ll stay close.”

“I didn’t ask for instructions.”

“No,” Duru said. “But you might need help.”

Another rush of water swept across the lower room. The hatchling squeaked and flattened itself against the ledge.

Ekin pulled off her jacket. Keeping both feet on the dry stair, she crouched and stretched toward the hatchling. It shied away at first, but there was nowhere else for it to go.

“Easy,” Ekin murmured. She spread the jacket over its back and sides, then gathered the covered hatchling carefully against her chest. Duru saw the whole awkward rescue, including the moment Ekin nearly lost her balance.

Duru caught Ekin’s arm and steadied her. Then she slid her hands beneath the bundled hatchling while Ekin climbed back to a wider step.

“Don’t drop it,” Ekin warned.

“I won’t.”

Ekin looked at Duru’s firm grip, then met her eyes. “All right. I’ve got you.”

Together they adjusted the handoff until Ekin could support the hatchling again and Duru could guide its covered body away from the stair’s edge.

They climbed side by side, carrying it between them. At the upper room, the mother dragon lowered her head. The hatchling wriggled free of the jacket and hurried to her.

Ekin remained beside Duru. The storm still shook the lighthouse, but the space between the two girls no longer felt quite so sharp.

“Thanks,” Ekin said quietly.

Duru gave one small nod. “We did it
